entities.summary:
Flavius Josephus, a prominent Roman-Jewish historian of the 1st century CE, stands as the most comprehensive surviving chronicler of the First Jewish-Roman War (66–73 CE) and the pivotal destruction of the Second Temple in Jerusalem. Born Joseph ben Mattathias in 37 CE in Jerusalem, then part of the Roman province of Judea, he hailed from an aristocratic priestly family with Hasmonean royal lineage, granting him unique insight into the intricate political and religious dynamics of his era. His seminal works, particularly *The Jewish War* (circa 75 CE) and *Antiquities of the Jews* (circa 93 CE), offer an unparalleled, though often contentious, narrative of Judean history and its complex relationship with the Roman Empire.

Initially serving as a Jewish military commander in Galilee during the early stages of the Great Revolt, Josephus was captured by the Romans in 67 CE at Jotapata. Following his capture, he transitioned to become an interpreter and intermediary for the Roman general Vespasian—whom he famously predicted would become emperor—and later for Vespasian's son, Titus. This controversial shift in allegiance allowed him to directly witness the siege and subsequent destruction of Jerusalem in 70 CE, experiences meticulously documented in *The Jewish War*. His *Antiquities of the Jews* further elaborates on Jewish history from creation up to the outbreak of the war, aiming to present Jewish culture and traditions favorably to a Greco-Roman audience.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Josephus's works are the principal surviving historical source for the First Jewish-Roman War and the destruction of the Second Temple, an event that profoundly reshaped Jewish identity and religious practice for millennia. His narratives also provide critical, albeit biased, insights into early Christianity and the broader socio-political landscape of the Roman East.
